absent: Concrete TLB flush primitives and cache maintenance implementations behind generic dispatch.
Gather allocation, full flush versus TLB-only flush split, batch reclamation, and teardown sequencing.
Folio release backing action and large-folio order helpers beyond the order query shown.
Low-level high-memory slot management, address translation, and indexed unmap mechanics.
Locking and ordering for concurrent gather, queue, and page-table mutation beyond the unshare note.
Configuration-dependent variants of gather storage, flush merging, and architecture hooks.
Reverse-map delay handling and table-batch freeing behavior.

findings.text: Gather context for batched invalidation tracks a target address space, an address interval, a whole-space optimization marker, a forced full-flush marker, a freed-tables marker, a delayed reverse-map marker, per-level cleared markers for four table levels, cached area attributes for executable huge and special frame mappings, two sharing-transition markers for shared huge tables, a batch counter, and optional table-batch and page-batch storage with an optional page-size record.
Small folio holder records occupancy and iteration positions plus a drained indicator and a fixed-capacity pointer array. Occupancy and iteration start empty and occupancy grows by insertion.

Queue segment embeds a folio holder with a parallel per-slot order record, links to next and previous segments, two independent per-slot mark words, and request plus debug identifiers. Capacity follows the batch capacity and is validated against mark-word width.
Batch and queue segment capacity is thirty one slots.

Range bookkeeping widens the tracked interval to cover each supplied address and length. Reset establishes an empty interval, or an inverted sentinel for whole-space operation, and clears table and level and sharing-transition markers while preserving cached area attributes across intermediate flushes.

One build flushes the whole address space whenever any interval was recorded. Another build flushes the whole space for whole-space or forced-full states and otherwise performs a ranged flush described by a synthesized area carrying cached executable and huge attributes. The TLB-only path does nothing unless some table, level, or sharing marker indicates work, then flushes and resets the interval.

Entering an area caches whether it is huge and whether it is executable, and accumulates a sticky record of special frame mappings across areas. Whole-space mode skips caching and cache maintenance. Leaving an area normally checkpoints TLB-only state to avoid growth across gaps and to keep cached attributes consistent, unless whole-space mode or a merge-areas build is active.
Huge-area determination at area level delegates to a flag-set query that tests a designated huge bit in a bitmap. A build without huge support always reports not huge.

Cleared state is tracked separately per table level together with interval widening. Effective unmap granularity prefers the smallest cleared level from page upward through three larger levels, with size as two raised to the selected shift. Releasing lower-level tables records a range at the parent level and marks tables freed. Unsharing a shared table records a parent-sized range.

Active unmap page size is remembered. Recording a different size while one is pending triggers an intermediate gather flush unless in whole-space or forced-full state, then the new size is stored. This applies only when the page-size tracking option is present.

Batch start clears occupancy, iteration position, and drained state, while reinit preserves drained state. Occupancy, remaining space, fullness, and segment counts derive from occupancy versus capacity. Insertion stores a folio and updates occupancy, with queue variants additionally snapshotting folio order and optionally setting the first mark. Iteration returns entries in order and signals exhaustion by absence. Accessors expose stored folio, snapped order, and size derived from page size and order. Clearing a slot empties the pointer and both marks.
Each queue segment maintains two independent one-bit-per-slot mark sets with separate test, set, and clear operations indexed by slot number.

Persistent mapping may sleep and uses a direct address for low memory while delegating high memory to a separate high path followed by an architecture hook. Unmapping may sleep and acts only for high memory. Local page mappings use a default protection unless an explicit-protection variant is used. Number and folio variants map by frame number or by folio plus offset preserving intra-page displacement. A panic-safe local query returns a direct address for low memory and absence for high memory. Indexed unmap releases local mappings, with helpers for address-to-page translation, unused-slot flushing, fork handling, and map-state assertion.

Atomic mappings disable preemption, or migration on realtime builds, and disable page faults around the local mapping operation. Frame-number atomic mapping follows the same guarding. Unmapping releases the local mapping then reenables faults and preemption or migration. A no-high-memory build maps atomically by direct address without entering the local mapping path, with a protection-parameterized variant delegating to the plain atomic path.
Headers use standard inclusion guards to prevent multiple inclusion.

Gather starts in whole-space or ranged mode with an empty interval. Per-area entry caches attributes and maintains caches. Removals widen the interval and set level or table markers. Area exit normally checkpoints TLB-only state. Special mappings force a checkpoint before unlinking. Page-size change may force a checkpoint. Shared-table finalization flushes pending invalidations when any unsharing occurred and performs a global walker wait only on transition to exclusive ownership.

Removal interfaces cover single entries, contiguous runs, size-tiered huge entries selecting the level by magnitude, and fixed-size PMD and PUD entries. Each widens the tracked interval at the appropriate level and invokes an architecture hook that is empty generically. Table descriptors use a common table-removal path, while per-level table-free helpers combine parent-level range recording with the freed-tables marker and an architecture free hook.

Unsharing decrements a shared-user count and observes whether sharing remains via an atomic counter. The caller must exclude concurrent unsharing combined with exclusive reuse until the shared-table flush routine has run. Becoming the exclusive owner additionally requires a global wait that drains concurrent fast page-table walkers before reuse.

Special frame mappings lack normal frame tracking, so unlinking such an area can race with a concurrent range unmap that observes neither the area nor the pending invalidation and returns early. A sticky indicator records whether such an area contributed pending work, and unlink preparation flushes TLB-only state when set.

Previously shared tables may be modified and reused, even outside huge-page context, once locks are dropped, so the unsharer must flush translations immediately and the final unsharer must wait for fast walkers. Builds without a separate table-sync wait rely on the TLB flush to provide needed ordering. Entry-change predicates for normal and huge PMD entries conservatively always request a flush. Unsharing validates that the table was shared, with build-dependent warning or compile-time check behavior.

Generic header exposes inline batching operations for range bookkeeping, per-area lifecycle, per-level invalidation recording, entry and table removal, table freeing, unmap granularity query, page-size tracking, and shared-table finalization.

Inline folio batch and queue operations are exposed for initialization, occupancy query, insertion, ordered iteration, conditional release, slot access, order and size query, mark manipulation, and segment linkage state.

Inline high-memory operations are exposed for persistent map and unmap, local map variants by page folio number and protection with indexed unmap, atomic map variants with paired unmap, address-to-page translation, unused-slot flushing, fork handling, and map-state assertion.
